newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Rival Afghan militias claim northern territory.
newsitem.headline: Rival Afghan militias claim northern territory.

text.p: Claims and counter-claims by rival Afghan militias left the situation in northern Afghanistan unclear three days after an opposition commander apparently changed sides and joined the purist Islamic Taleban.
The Taleban say they have captured two provinces -- Faryab and Sar-i-Pul -- with the help of the mutinous commander and his troops, and are still advancing.

The rebel governor of Sar-i-Pul confirmed to the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) on Wednesday night that Taleban fighters were in Sar-i-Pul, but there are still questions over the extent of the Taleban penetration into Faryab.

An opposition spokesman said on Wednesday Taleban forces had not entered Faryab province and negotiations were continuing to try to persuade the mutinous commander, General Abdul Malik, to rejoin the anti-Taleban alliance led by General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The revolt against Dostum has given the Taleban, who captured the capital Kabul last September, a new chance to impose their rule in a country devastated by decades of war.
A Taleban spokesman said on Wednesday all the mutineers had been absorbed into the ranks of the Taleban militia.

"All the mujahedin and military personnel who switched sides are now part of the Islamic Army of Afghanistan (the Taleban). The forces in Faryab have been organised into the ranks of the Islamic army," said Maulawi Wakhil Ahmed Motawakhil.

Motawakhil said Taleban forces had entered Maimana, the provincial capital of Faryab, and were advancing towards one of the opposition's most important bases, Shebergan, where much of the opposition air force is based.

But according to opposition spokesman Dr Abdullah (one name), Taleban forces had occupied only one district in Faryab, and had met opposition from the mutineers in doing so. He said the province was still controlled by Malik.

"The whole province is still controlled by Malik except for one district. Today the Taleban entered Qaisar district (in the west of Faryab), where fighting took place. Besides the reports of fighting in Qaisar it has been calm today, there haven't been any significant changes," Abdullah said on Wednesday night.

An aid worker in Dostum's stronghold of Mazar-e-Sharif told Reuters on Thursday he believed that some Taleban had been moving through Faryab to the opposition's new front line in Jawzjan province, but added that reports he was receiving said the rebels had asked the Taleban to move back.

"We have heard of some movements through Faryab by Taleban vehicles towards Jawzjan, but we hear that the rebels have asked the Taleban to move back to their original front line as they prefer to keep control on their own." said the aid worker.
Abdullah told Reuters that Malik and his fighters had not finally decided to join the Taleban.

"From one side they want to do something against Dostum and from the other they don't want the Taleban," Abdullah told Reuters by satellite telephone from the opposition-held areanorth of Afghanistan.
Abdullah said the opposition was still negotiating with Malik.

"Negotiations are still going on, but so far there has been no agreement. Malik's position should be clear, he cannot maintain a position where he is not part of the Taleban and not part of Dostum's forces," he said.
However, Western observers in the north reported that the opposition was digging trenches on the border of Jawzjan and Faryab provinces.
Abdullah said there had been some problems in other areas of the country and that security had been strengthened in the town.
The aid worker in Mazar-e-Sharif said checkpoints had been set up on all roads leading to the town.

He said Mazar-e-Sharif was generally calm on Thursday morning and the Afghan currency, the Afghani, a barometer of public opinion on the security situation, had bounced back to 68,000 to the dollar after touching a low of 90,000 on Tuesday.
